results.finalAssistantText:
**Short answer: nothing broke in the quarter. The stock was priced for a bigger quarter than the one NVIDIA delivered — and for a margin line that went the wrong way.**

$NVDA fell -6.38% [C37] to close at USD 117.59 [C36]. That is -8.02 USD per share [C38] on 24,848,000,000 diluted shares [C39] — a decline of -199,281,087,543 USD in market value [C40].

## The beat was real, just smaller and slower

- Non-GAAP EPS of 0.68 USD per share [C59:actual] against a 0.63 USD estimate [C59:estimate]; revenue of 30,040,000,000 USD [C49].
- The surprise has shrunk for four straight quarters: 30.4% [C58:2023-07-31] → 19.6% [C58:2023-10-31] → 11.9% [C58:2024-01-31] → 9.5% [C58:2024-04-30] → **7.9%** [C58:2024-07-31]. A stock at this multiple is financed by the *change* in the beat, not the beat.
- Guidance of 32.5 billion USD ±2% [E11] is 8.19% [C53] quarter over quarter and 79.36% [C54] year over year — against the 122.40% just reported [C55]. Growth roughly halves.
- Gross margin: 75.1% GAAP, down from 78.4% [E11]; non-GAAP 75.7% from 78.9%. Q3 is guided to 74.4% GAAP, with non-GAAP at 75.0% ±50bp [E12] — a band of 74.5% [C56] to 75.5% [C57]. Management blamed "inventory provisions for low-yielding Blackwell material" and a richer mix of new products [E12]. The mask change to improve yields, and a Blackwell ramp that now begins in Q4 with only "several billion dollars" of Blackwell revenue in that quarter [E12], pushed the volume inflection toward calendar 2025.

That is the tradeoff in one line: demand is intact, while margin and timing got worse exactly when the price required both to improve. At USD 117.59 [C36] the stock trades at 55.23x trailing GAAP EPS [C51] and 30.34x trailing revenue [C52], on a market cap of 2,921,876,220,608 USD [C41]. In-line guidance cannot hold a 30x sales multiple.

## The AI trade is not what sold off

The complex held on the day: $SMH -1.24% [C60:SMH], $AMD -0.59% [C60:AMD], $AVGO -0.79% [C60:AVGO], $TSM -0.03% [C60:TSM], $SMCI 1.20% [C60:SMCI], $MSFT 0.61% [C60:MSFT], $SPY 0.01% [C60:SPY]. The Dow closed at a record and Reuters called the guide "largely in-line" [E13]. This was a single-stock de-rating — profit-taking in the one name that had run — not a sector-wide exit from AI.

It is also ordinary weather for this stock: seven separate drawdowns of at least ten percent in 2024 [C46], a maximum close-to-close drawdown of -27.05% [C44], 57.06% annualised volatility [C45], still up 144.12% year to date [C43], and now -16.46% [C42] from the June intraday high. It fell -28.81% [C47] into the 5 August low and rebounded 38.50% [C48] in seventeen sessions.

## On "cutting losses"

I can't tell you to sell or hold, and I won't. Two things I can tell you. First, I have **no view of your holdings**: no portfolio account is linked in this session, so I don't know your cost basis, size or concentration — and "losses" implies an entry above USD 117.59 [C36] in a stock still up 144.12% this year [C43]. Second, the question this print poses is narrower than "is AI over": was your reason for owning it volume growth at expanding margins, or the multi-year build-out of accelerated data-centre capacity? The first leg weakened this quarter and is now a bet on a Q4 Blackwell ramp; the second was not contradicted, only delayed and taxed. What settles it is whether Q3 gross margin holds inside 74.5% [C56] to 75.5% [C57] and Blackwell ships in Q4 as promised [E12] — and how a -27.05% [C44] drawdown would sit against the size of the position you actually hold.

This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
## What actually happened

It wasn't the beat that got sold — it was the guide, and specifically the second derivative.

- **Revenue guided to $32.5bn** ±2% for Q3 [E9] — above the quarter just reported, but implying only **8.19%** sequential growth [C12] against **15.34%** actually delivered in Q2 [C2:2024-07-28] [E3]. The guide halves NVDA's sequential growth rate in one step.
- **Non-GAAP gross margin guided down to 75.0%** [E10], from **75.7%** in Q2 [E9] and **78.9%** in Q1 [E19] — a fall of **−3.9%** [C15] from the peak. Management attributes it to "inventory provisions for low-yielding Blackwell material and a higher mix of new products" [E10]. Real cost, real explanation, but no recovery is guided.
- **The beat is shrinking every quarter**: **7.94%** [C6], then **9.48%** [C9:2024-04-30], **11.93%** [C9:2024-01-31], **19.64%** [C9:2023-10-31], versus **30.43%** [C10] six quarters ago [E6].
- Reuters' framing is exact: "a largely in-line forecast failed to impress investors" who were "accustomed to the chipmaker beating expectations by massive margins" [E11].

The reported quarter itself was clean: revenue of **$30.04bn** [E3:revenue:2024-07-28] was **122.40%** higher than a year earlier [C1], and non-GAAP EPS of **0.68** [E6:dilutedEps:2024-07-31] cleared a **0.63** [E6:estimatedEps:2024-07-31] consensus.

## Is the AI trade falling apart?

The tape says no, and this is the decisive evidence: on the same session **$AMD −0.59%** [C41:AMD], **$AVGO −0.79%** [C41:AVGO], **$TSM −0.03%** [C41:TSM], **$SMCI +1.20%** [C41:SMCI] [E4] — a peer median of **−0.31%** [C42], while **$NVDA fell −6.38%** [C26]. The Dow closed at a record high that day [E11]. NVDA underperformed its peer median by **−6.07%** [C43]. A sector unwind does not look like that.

It's also within this stock's normal behaviour: the shares fell 6% or more on **8** sessions in the price window [C48], with a **−27.05%** max drawdown over that window [C49] [E5], and it sits **−3.45%** below its first post-split close on 10 June [C50]. The de-rating landed on the multiple: **53.2x** trailing non-GAAP earnings [C24], **1.60%** FCF yield [C34].

## On "cut my losses and sell"

I can't answer that as posed. `portfolio_get` returned no accounts — I have no view of your holdings, cost basis, position weight or horizon.

What I can give you is the test the data supports:

- **Demand is intact**: Data Center **$26.3bn**, up 154% year on year [E9], cash conversion of **0.87x** [C17] [E16/E3] — a real ramp, not pulled-forward revenue. Even the new guide implies **79.36%** growth [C13] [E9].
- **Pace and margin are not**: shrinking beats, halved sequential guidance, and a gross margin guided down rather than up.
- **Falsifiers to watch**: Q3 revenue below the **$31.85bn** low end [C14:low] [E9]; Q4 gross margin guided below 75.0% [E10] with no yield-recovery path; the Blackwell provision repeating; any cut to hyperscaler capex — the actual source of that Data Center quarter [E9].

**In short:** NVIDIA beat and sold off because it guided to half the sequential growth [C12] and a lower margin [C15], with no margin recovery yet promised — a re-pricing of pace, not a verdict on AI. Peers flat to up [C41:AMD] [C41:AVGO] [C41:TSM] [C41:SMCI] and a record-high Dow [E11] argue strongly against "the AI trade is falling apart." Against that, a **53.2x** trailing multiple [C24] leaves little room for further deceleration. Whether today is noise or a warning depends on your entry price and horizon, which I can't see.

This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
**On stealing Nike's lunch — partly, and less than the mall suggests.** The challengers are too small to explain a $51.4 billion [E20] company stalling: On's whole calendar-2023 revenue is 3.5% [C48] of Nike's fiscal-2024 revenue and HOKA's wholesale line is 2.2% [C49]. But they are taking the increments. HOKA's wholesale revenue rose 21.6% [C29], adding $200.2m [C30] in its fiscal 2024 — more than Nike's entire net revenue increase of $183m [C3] — and On added CHF 570m [C31] in 2023. The sharpest evidence is the channel both bet on: On's direct-to-consumer sales grew 50.9% [C51] while Nike Direct fell 8% [C50] in the fourth quarter. Most of Nike's trouble is still self-inflicted: growth decelerated from +19.1% [C45] in FY21 to +0.3% [C47] in the February quarter, and gross margin fell −2.46 percentage points [C41] in FY23.

**Bargain or trap — neither, it's priced for stabilisation.** At $75.43 [E11] the stock is 20.2x [C4] trailing FY24 EPS of $3.73 [C1], with net debt effectively nil [C9], a 4.2% [C10] free cash flow yield, and nine-month free cash flow up 45.8% [C16]. That is not distress. But the multiple rises as earnings fall — at FY23's EPS of $3.23 [E4] the same price is 23.4x [C5]. Deckers, growing 18.2% [C44], trades at 32.2x [C7]; Nike's −37.2% discount to that [C56] is roughly the growth gap. On a common window since 12 February, Nike is −29.6% [C21], On +23.8% [C22], Deckers +11.2% [C23].

Three citation caveats: the consensus estimate of $0.83 a share [E13:estimatedEps:2024-05-31], fiscal-2024 revenue of $51.4 billion [E20] and the close of $75.43 [E11] are sound in substance but had their inline citations flagged in the original report, so treat those three as sourced-by-series rather than by single cell. On's and Deckers' margins come from their key-metric tables [E5, E6].

Limits: Nike's FY25 guidance is sourced only to Morningstar's 2 July note, which cut fair value to $124 [E25] and cited "a projected mid-single-digit sales decline in fiscal 2025"; the 8-K body was not captured. The "five-year low" claim is unverifiable because price history here starts in January 2024 — the 2020 trough was lower. No market-share data exists in these sources, so displacement is inferred from growth and margin differentials, and the CHF-to-USD comparison is unconverted.

**Conclusion.** Nike's fall is real and dated: −19.98% [C17] on 28 June on 130m shares [C18], after a quarter that beat on EPS. On and Hoka did not take Nike's lunch at scale — 3.5% [C48] and 2.2% [C49] of its revenue — but they took the growth and the direct-to-consumer momentum, each adding more absolute revenue than Nike did [C3, C30, C31]. That makes the stock a bet on Nike's own reset, not on the challengers failing. At 20.2x [C4] falling earnings, with a net-neutral balance sheet [C9] and a 4.2% [C10] free cash flow yield, the price assumes revenue stops declining within about a year; if the reset runs longer, the multiple expands into the decline and today's level is not a floor. Remaining uncertainty: Nike's own FY25 guidance and true share data were unavailable, so trough timing is unproven in either direction.

This is research, not investment advice.

The corrections are in: the sensitivity row labels are 6.4748% [C162] and 8.4748% [C163] — the base WACC of 7.4748% [C161] shifted one point either way — and the combined challenger share is 6.12% [C166], not "under 6%".

**The mall is seeing a real trend, but it isn't yet a transfer of Nike's business.** On's revenue compounded at 60.94% [C93] a year from FY2019–FY2023 and HOKA's wholesale line grew 21.63% [C97] last fiscal year, against Nike's 0.36% [C148]. But On's entire FY2023 revenue is 3.92% [C109] of Nike's and HOKA's wholesale line is 2.2% [C110]. In one year the two added about $839m of revenue [C153] versus Nike's $183m [C149].

**The decisive tell is the channel split.** In the quarter Nike just reported, NIKE Direct fell 8% while wholesale grew 5% (8% currency-neutral) [E19]. If On and Hoka were taking shelf space, wholesale would be the line bleeding. Instead the damage sits in Nike's own direct business — the channel it spent four years pulling product into. That points at a self-inflicted reset plus a lifestyle-franchise downturn, not a competitive rout.

**On bargain versus trap:** $75.43 [E5] is 20.22x [C118] the FY2024 EPS its own quarters add up to (3.73 [C111]), with a 4.23% [C119] free cash flow yield. My DCF on FY2023 free cash flow gives 66.57 [C125], so the price is a 13.3% [C129] premium — a pause is priced, not a decline.

**Limits:** the FY2024 cash-flow statement isn't in the captured filings, so the DCF base year is stale and inventory-depressed; the five-year-low claim is unverifiable here (what is verified is a 2024 low of 75.24 [C87]); and the sensitivity grid runs from 51.83 [C136] to 93.98 [C132] a share, wider than the gap between price and base case.

**Conclusion.** The share-loss story is directionally true and numerically small: On grew 46.64% [C94] and HOKA 21.63% [C97] while Nike went flat at 0.36% [C148], yet together they are 6.12% [C166] of Nike's revenue. Nike's damage sits in its own direct channel — Q4 NIKE Direct down 8% against wholesale up 5% [E19] — which is why a quarter that beat EPS estimates by 19.28% [E27] still fell 19.98% [C84]. At $75.43 [E5] the stock is not cheap: 20.22x [C118] trailing earnings, a 4.23% [C119] free cash flow yield, a 13.3% [C129] premium to base-case value of 66.57 [C125], with the price implying 4.22% [C139] ten-year free cash flow growth. That is a pause priced, not a franchise broken — neither bargain nor trap. Unresolved: FY2024 cash flow, which the base year lacks, and category-level share, which no filing here carries.

results.finalAssistantText:
**The short answer: one company has cash, one company has a contract, and they're different companies.**

- **$TLN** is the only name where a hyperscaler has actually paid. AWS released $300 million [E22] from escrow on 23 August 2024 [E22], tied to milestones enabling the campus to reach 960 MW [E22] of consumption. Its 960 MW [E33] Susquehanna PPA was still pre-delivery — Talen said it "look[s] forward to executing on power sales under the PPA" [E22].
- **$CEG** has the only 20-year [E10] hyperscaler PPA for nuclear electrons — Microsoft, its largest ever [E10], supporting the 835 MW [E10] Three Mile Island restart. Online 2028 [E10]. No cash from Microsoft yet.
- **$VST** earns $14.43 billion [C1:VST] TTM but from wholesale markets, not Big Tech. **$SMR** earns $13.86 million [C1:SMR], from DOE and a Romanian utility [E37]. **$OKLO** earns $0 [C1:OKLO].

Where the money actually comes from: PJM cleared Talen's 6,820 MW [E30] at $269.92 per MW-day [E30], about $672 million annualised [C11] — roughly 0.90x [C13] of guided 2024 EBITDA [E29]. The grid pays first.

---

**Conclusion.** The narrative that nuclear is being bankrolled by Big Tech is, on this date, supported by only two disclosed transactions [E10][E22]. Talen has received the only material hyperscaler cash — $300 million [C14] — but it was paid for a data-center campus, not electrons. Constellation holds the only long-term nuclear PPA with a hyperscaler, 835 MW [C16] for 20 years [E10], with delivery starting 2028 [E10]. Neither discloses its contract price, so the margin uplift is unverifiable from public filings. Meanwhile the operators' earnings come from capacity scarcity: Talen cleared 6,820 MW [E30] at $269.92 per MW-day [E30], about $672 million annualised [C11], roughly 0.90x [C13] its guided 2024 EBITDA [E29]. The genuine bottleneck is regulatory, not technological — FERC has Talen's co-location amendment under a deficiency letter after an Exelon/AEP protest [E23][E24]. The pre-revenue names have no hyperscaler revenue and fund themselves through 24.2% [C17] and 45.3% [C18] year-over-year dilution. This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
The report is open. Here is what the filings actually show.

**Only one name is cashing checks.** Talen ($TLN) received $650m of gross proceeds from AWS for the Cumulus data-centre campus in March 2024, and the $300m escrow was released and paid on 23 August 2024 [E37] [E20]. It also has a PPA to supply up to 960 MW from Susquehanna, stepping up in 120 MW increments, with AWS able to cap at 480 MW [E37]. That said, Talen's own release still says it looks *forward* to executing power sales under the PPA [E20], and the enabling co-location amendment was under protest at FERC from AEP and Exelon [E21] — cash received, structure contested.

**The famous deal pays nothing yet.** Constellation's ($CEG) 20-year PPA with Microsoft covers the full output of the restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1, subject to regulatory approvals [E9], with the plant expected online in 2028 [E26]. At a mid-range power price that contract is about 2.6% of Constellation's $19.97bn trailing revenue [C12] [C22] — yet the stock moved 22.3% in one session on the news [C17]. The market repriced the fleet's future pricing power, not this contract's cash flow.

**Vistra ($VST) is in the Big Tech chain, but not for nuclear:** 200 MW with Amazon in Texas and 405 MW with Microsoft in Illinois, both solar, both in construction [E30], against $14.43bn of trailing revenue [C23].

**The pure plays have no contracts.** NuScale ($SMR) earned $13.9m over twelve months [C21], with Q2 revenue down 83.3% year on year [C7] and about 3.2 quarters of cash at the current operating burn [C19]; its release describes "conversations," not orders [E27]. Oklo ($OKLO) reported zero revenue in every quarter, carries going-concern language, and holds $294.6m [E35] [E15] — roughly 16.6 quarters of runway [C20].

Qualification: the 835 MW and 960 MW capacity inputs, the 90% capacity factor, the $60–100/MWh price band and the quarterly operating loss are stated in the report as declared inputs rather than figures matched to a single evidence entry, and the report flags them accordingly. Contract prices are undisclosed in both nuclear PPAs, so all contract revenue is scenario arithmetic.

**Conclusion.** If the question is who is being paid by Big Tech now, the answer is Talen, on an asset sale, with contracted generation revenue still ahead of it. Constellation holds the strongest strategic contract in the sector but collects nothing until a 2028 restart clears regulators, and the same contract is immaterial to its revenue base while being plausibly worth about four-fifths of Talen's 2024 EBITDA guidance midpoint at full ramp [C13]. Vistra's Big Tech money is solar, not nuclear. NuScale and Oklo have no Big Tech revenue at all — NuScale's revenue is falling and its cash covers a few quarters of burn, Oklo has none and says so in going-concern language. The uncomfortable implication for "bet big on nuclear": every binding dollar traced here goes to owners of already-built or restartable reactors, not to reactor designers, and the entire complex has already re-rated on announcements rather than cash. The uncertainty that would settle it is disclosed PPA pricing and the FERC ruling on co-location.

This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
**Two names have real hyperscaler contracts. One of them has actually been paid.**

- **$TLN — Amazon/AWS.** The August 2024 release confirms the **$300M** escrowed tranche of the Cumulus campus purchase price was released and paid to Talen once milestones allowed development to 960 MW [E34] of consumption [E12]. The investor deck sets out a Susquehanna PPA for up to 960 MW [E34] direct-connect carbon-free power, commitments rising 120 MW [E34] a year with an acceleration option, fixed price over ten-year terms repriced at market [E34]. That 960 MW [E34] equals **43.1%** [C15] of Susquehanna's 2,228 MW [E34] owned capacity. Contracted capacity, not a rendering.
- **$CEG — Microsoft.** A signed **20-year** [E7] PPA, Constellation's largest ever, tied to restarting Three Mile Island Unit 1 as the Crane Clean Energy Center, with the plant expected online in **2028** [E11] and the restart subject to NRC approval after safety and environmental review [E7][E11]. Genuine contract, zero revenue today: you are buying a 2028 cash flow, discounted for permitting and restart risk.

**Everybody else is selling a story.** $OKLO recognised **$0** [C20] of revenue across all four [C21] quarters to June 2024, while its own 10-Q raises substantial doubt about continuing as a going concern against $294.6M [E40] of cash and marketable securities. $SMR has **$13.9M** [C5:SMR] of trailing revenue against a market cap near $1B [C7] — **70.4x** [C8:SMR] revenue, versus **4.1x** [C8:CEG] for $CEG and **2.7x** [C8:VST] for $VST. $VST earns **$14.4B** [C5:VST] from an operating fleet but had no disclosed hyperscaler nuclear supply contract in anything I could retrieve through this date.

**The premise is doing work it hasn't earned.** Both real deals are PJM, Pennsylvania, and both sell output from reactors built in the 1980s or a unit retired in 2019 — speed to existing interconnection. Talen's own deck says serving data-centre growth "requires a balance of direct-connected and grid-connected solutions" [E34]. That is a capacity-scarcity and repricing story, not proof that nuclear is the only answer.

**The risk nobody prices:** PJM's amended interconnection agreement to sell up to 480 MW [E13] directly to co-located load was protested by Exelon and AEP, and FERC issued a deficiency letter in August 2024 [E13] asking for more information. Part of the AWS contract's economics rests on permission that is still contested.

**Qualifying the report's verification notes:** the Crane nameplate capacity, the two PPA price points behind my revenue scenarios, and NuScale's quarterly operating loss are unverified against my evidence set — treat the report's PPA revenue ranges as declared scenarios, not disclosed economics. Market caps use last-reported diluted share counts [C7], so they are approximations.

### Conclusion

Only $CEG and $TLN have signed, disclosed nuclear supply agreements with a hyperscaler as of 23 September 2024. $TLN is the only one that has banked money: a $300M [E12] escrowed tranche released in August, backing a PPA for up to 960 MW [E34] at Susquehanna. $CEG's 20-year [E7] Microsoft contract is real but delivers nothing until a 2028 [E11] restart clears the NRC. The pre-revenue developers are a different asset class entirely — $OKLO at $0 [C20] revenue with going-concern language [E40], $SMR at 70.4x [C8:SMR] trailing revenue against 2.7-4.1x [C8:VST][C8:CEG] for the operating utilities. For your question, that means the "nuclear" label tells you almost nothing; what separates these names is contracted cash flow versus narrative, and even the winners' economics are hidden behind undisclosed PPA prices. Remaining uncertainty: FERC's ruling on co-location [E13] and NRC timing at Crane, either of which can change the answer without any change in the story.

This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
**No — and the catch shows up in the sponsor's own numbers, not just in the risk language.**

**Month one works; that's the trap.** $500,000 [A13] targeting $20,000 a month [A14] is $240,000 a year [C45], a 48% payout [C7]. At $15.08 [E1], the full amount buys 33,156 shares [C46], and $0.6448 a share [A36] pays $21,379 a month [C47].

**What the 51% is made of.** YieldMax's 5 June 2024 announcement puts $TSLY at a 51.06% distribution rate [A37] against a 4.20% 30-day SEC yield [A3] — a 46.86-point gap [C15]. The "rate" annualises the latest payment over NAV; the SEC yield is what the portfolio earns [E4]. In the audited period to 31 October 2023, $TSLY distributed $7.93 a share [A9], of which $7.26 [A10] was return of capital — 91.55% [C11] — while NAV per share fell from $20.00 [A7] to $11.09 [A8]. Distributions equalled 39.65% of the starting NAV [C12], yet total per-share value change was −4.90% [C14]: a ~40% payout year that mostly handed your own capital back and left a smaller base to pay the next one from.

**The sustainability bar.** Holding capital and the cheque flat at a 51.06% payout requires a 51.06% annual total return [C30]. With a flat total return, $500,000 becomes $14,038 in five years [C48] and the cheque $1,220 a month [C49]. At a 4.00% withdrawal rate [A29] the same capital pays $1,667 a month [C32]; $20,000 a month would need $6,000,000 [C41], which is 12× your target rate [C42].

**$MSTY is the more aggressive version.** A 106.33% distribution rate [A5] against a 0.00% 30-day SEC yield [A6], on a fund whose price history starts 22 February 2024 [E6]. It fell 39.71% peak-to-trough in the five weeks to 1 May [C18] while $MSTR fell 46.42% [C20]; and when $MSTR rose 109.71% [C21], $MSTY's price rose 39.01% before distributions [C22]. That gap is the capped upside funding the premium.

---

**Conclusion.** The distributions are real cash, but not a yield you can bank on: much of each payment is option premium and return of capital, and the dollar amount is set monthly against a capital base that shrinks whenever the reference stock does not rise. $TSLY's first audited period paid out 39.65% of starting NAV [C12] with 91.55% of it your own money [C11], leaving per-share value −4.90% [C14] and a NAV per share cut from $20.00 [A7] to $11.09 [A8]. Sustaining $20,000 a month [A14] requires a 51.06% annual total return [C30]; at a flat return the capital is $14,038 after five years and the cheque $1,220 a month [C48] [C49]. $MSTY pairs a 106.33% rate [A5] with a 0.00% SEC yield [A6] and a 3.8-month record — the same mechanism, less history, far more volatility. Uncertainty that remains: no audited annual report for $MSTY, my reading of the 26 February price gap as a share consolidation is inference, and the five-year paths illustrate the payout formula rather than forecast either fund.

This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
**The arithmetic is fine — that's the problem.** $500,000 [U1] of $TSLY at $15.08 [E1] buys 33,156.5 shares [C1] paying $0.6448 in June [E5] = **$21,379/month** [C3], which the issuer would quote as a 51.06% distribution rate on NAV [E5]. Your $20,000/month target [U3] is a 48% annual payout rate [C26]. It works on paper because the payout rate is enormous, not because the income is earned.

**The catch, from the fund's own filings.** The same issuer release shows $TSLY's 30-day SEC yield at 4.20% [E5] and $MSTY's at **0.00%** [E5] against a 106.33% distribution rate [E5]. In $TSLY's financial highlights, net investment income was $0.26/share [A18] versus $3.64/share distributed [A19] in the six months to 30 April 2024 — 7.1% coverage [C11]; in the first period $7.26 of $7.93 per share was return of capital [A13][A23], which is 91.6% [C12]. NAV went $20.00 [A21] → $11.09 [A22] and total return including all distributions was **−4.9%** [C13], after distributing 39.65% of starting capital [C21]. Income genuinely earned on $500,000 [U1] of $TSLY: about $1,437/month [C24]. To sustain a 51.06% payout [E5] plus the 0.99% expense ratio [A24], the strategy must earn ~52.3%/year [C22] out of capped upside [E7]. $MSTY adds 94.6% volatility [C15] and a −39.7% drawdown in ten weeks [C17], on a $MSTR closed at $1,495.54 [E1].

Note: $500,000 [U1] and $20,000 [U3] are your stated figures, unverified; per-share distributions come from the June release [E5] and the filing text [E6]. My daily $TSLY price series has an unreconciled step on 26 Feb 2024, so I used filed NAV rather than price history.

**Conclusion.** The $20,000/month [U3] is achievable as cash flow and is not a return on capital: 91.6% [C12] of $TSLY's first-period distributions were return of capital, net investment income covered 7.1% [C11] of the payout, and the fund's first twelve months produced −4.9% total return [C13] while NAV fell 44.6% [C20]. Mechanically, distribution rate minus NAV erosion equals your total return, and only that compounds — so a 48% withdrawal rate [C26] spends the same capital that generates the cheque, and each month's income shrinks with the base. $MSTY is the same machinery on a more violent underlying: 0.00% SEC yield [E5], 106.33% payout rate [E5], −39.7% drawdown in ten weeks [C17]. What remains uncertain is direction — a sustained TSLA/MSTR rally would make these look good again for a while, as the six months to April 2024 did [E6], and I take no view on that. This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
Your $20,000-a-month target [U3] on $500,000 [U1] is arithmetically right and economically wrong, and the issuer's own June 2024 release shows why.

**The number that settles it.** $TSLY's distribution was $0.6448 [C36] per share, a stated distribution rate of 51.06% [E7] against a 4.20% [E7] 30-day SEC yield. $MSTY was $3.03 [C37] per share, a 106.33% [E7] distribution rate against a 0.00% [C46] 30-day SEC yield. That release defines the distribution rate as the last payout times twelve divided by NAV [E7] — a backward annualisation of one month, not what the portfolio earns. On the same arithmetic, 91.77% [C45] of $TSLY's payout was not covered by net investment income, and the corresponding share for $MSTY was effectively all of it [C46].

**What it pays, and what sustaining it requires.** $500,000 [U1] in $TSLY buys 33,156.5 [C38] shares, paying $21,379.31 [C39] in the June cycle — $256,551.72 [C40] annualised, or 51.31% [C4] of the position. $MSTY on the same capital is 16,972.2 [C5] shares and $51,425.66 [C41] for one month, annualising to 123.42% [C42]. For $TSLY to pay that rate and hold NAV it must earn 52.07% [C47] gross a year after its 1.01% [E11] total expense ratio — $5,050 [C48] on $500,000 [U1] — in a period when $TSLA's price change was −28.34% [C54] year to date.

**Where the money came from.** From 2024-02-26 to 2024-06-14, $TSLY's price change was −18.62% [C51], an annualised −49.84% [C52], against $TSLA's −10.73% [C53]. $500,000 [U1] invested on 2024-02-26 [C16] was worth $406,907.72 [C61] on 2024-06-14, a change of −$93,092.28 [C62], against a June distribution of $17,398.81 [C63] on those shares. At that decay rate the principal halves in 12.06 [C64] months. The structure explains the asymmetry: a synthetic covered call, "subject to a limit on potential investment gains" [E13] — upside capped, downside retained. Realised volatility ran 43.09% [C58] for $TSLY, 94.65% [C59] for $MSTY and 53.76% [C60] for $TSLA, with maximum drawdowns of −31.68% [C55], −39.71% [C56] and −42.82% [C57] across differing 2024 windows.

**Caveats.** Price change is not total return: earlier monthly distributions in that window are absent from my sources, so total return over it is uncomputed and likely somewhat better than the price figures imply. An unadjusted series shows a 104.98% [C49] two-session jump while $TSLA moved 3.87% [C50] — consistent with a reverse share split the filing record here does not confirm [E12]. And the headline rate rests on a single month's payout: the same release printed 20.94% [E7] for $XOMO and 101.82% [E7] for $NVDY.

The full analysis, including what you would receive versus what the capital did, is in the report open beside this.

**Conclusion.** The headline is a distribution rate on NAV, not a yield on assets: $TSLY's 30-day SEC yield was 4.20% [E7], $MSTY's was 0.00% [C46], and 91.77% [C45] of $TSLY's payout was uncovered by portfolio income. Paying that rate needs 52.07% [C47] gross a year to hold NAV while $TSLA moved −28.34% [C54]; the observed outcome was a −18.62% [C51] price change and −$93,092.28 [C62] of principal against $17,398.81 [C63] of distributions. Add capped upside [E13], volatility from 43.09% [C58] to 94.65% [C59], a payout recomputed monthly [E7], and $5,050 [C48] a year in fees per $500,000 [U1]. It is variable, partly self-funded, and not a coupon substitute. Remaining uncertainty: total return over the window is uncomputed and the reverse split is unconfirmed [E12].

This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
Your premise is half-right, and the half that's wrong is the dangerous half.

**The P/B is real — on shareholders' equity, not on the enterprise.** Intel closed at $20.11 [E3] against $27.00 of book value per share [C29], a 0.74x price-to-book [C30] on $115.2B of Intel shareholders' equity [E2]. Add back $48.3B of long-term debt [E2] and $5.21B of minority interests [C71], net of $11.3B of cash [E2], and enterprise value is $128.1B [C32] — 1.06x book equity [C33], with net debt of $37.0B [C34]. The equity is a levered slice of the asset base, priced at roughly par, not at a discount.

**Book value is not a floor because the burn is real.** Q2 revenue fell 0.9% year on year [C47] at a 35.4% gross margin [C45] and a −15.3% operating margin [C46], producing a net loss of $1.61B [C72]. Trailing twelve months: $11.5B of operating cash flow [C39] against $24.1B of capex [C40] equals −$12.6B of free cash flow [C41], a −14.7% FCF yield [C44]. On EV/EBITDA the shares sit at 13.1x [C43], not cheap — the D&A input there is annualised from the first half [A4]. The Q3 guide doesn't inflect: revenue of $12.5B to $13.5B [C74][C75], down 8.2% at the $13.0B midpoint versus the year-ago quarter [C76][C65], and a 34.5% GAAP gross margin [C66].

**The CHIPS money is a capex offset, not shareholder cash.** First-half 2024 additions to property, plant and equipment were $11.65B [C68]; capital-related government incentives received were $0.70B [C69], or 6.0% of capex [C70]. The foundry those fabs serve lost $2.83B at the operating line in a single quarter [C73]. Final award terms aren't verifiable from my sources for this date; a widely syndicated $7.865B page is dated into this window but carries October 2024 content, so I won't lean on it.

**On Buffett:** fear is measurable — 30.8% lost between the 1 August close and today [C78], and 54.8% below the 2024 closing high [C79] that stood at $44.52 [C77], with 55.3% annualised volatility [C53]. Greed requires a value estimate, and the value anchor here is missing: trailing twelve-month operating income is −$0.46B [C37]. The quote's precondition is also patience, and Intel just suspended a dividend worth 2.49% [C54] and cut 15% of roles to save $10B [E12].

**And the sizing point, which is the actual question:** "life savings" converts one company's foundry execution into your whole financial outcome, with $37.0B of net debt [C34] ranking ahead of you. Your portfolio record is empty [portfolio], so I can't see what fraction this would be — and a chart in the report has price points that didn't resolve against the evidence, so treat the path as directional rather than exact.

**Conclusion.** Intel is cheap on accounting book — 0.74x [C30] — and not cheap on what pays shareholders: 1.06x EV/book [C33], 13.1x EV/EBITDA [C43], a −14.7% FCF yield [C44], a dividend suspended [C54], and a foundry losing $2.83B a quarter [C73]. CHIPS incentives reached the cash flow statement at 6.0% of capex [C70] — a cost offset, not a transfer to equity holders. Fear is measurable at 54.8% below the high [C79] with 55.3% volatility [C53]; the value anchor Buffett's line requires is not, with trailing twelve-month operating income at −$0.46B [C37]. Reaching book requires +34% to $27.00 [C60][C62], but one more year at the current burn puts book at $24.06 [C56] and the same target at +20% [C61] — the floor moves down while you wait. What resolves it: disclosed external foundry customers, GAAP gross margin above roughly 40%, positive free cash flow, and clarity on grant versus loan. The remaining uncertainty is whether the turnaround lands at all, and over what horizon.

This is research, not investment advice.

results.finalAssistantText:
Intel filed the answer four days ago, in the Q2 release.

**The valuation leg is correct.** At $20.11 [C54] the shares trade at 0.74x [C57] Intel's reported stockholders' equity of $115,229M [C56], or 0.71x [C58] counting non-controlling interests. In late March the same measure was 1.77x [C59]. The de-rating came in three sessions: −5.50% [C82], −26.06% [C83], −6.38% [C84], for −54.83% [C85] from the 1 April close.

**The other two legs do not hold as stated.** Book value rose $9,256M [C61] in Q2 while the quarter produced a net loss of $1,610M [C86], funded by $11,861M [C62] of H1 partner contributions — 128% [C63] of that increase. Trailing free cash flow is −$12,584M [C67], a −14.67% [C70] yield, with capex at 2.09x [C72] operating cash flow and $34,273M [C88] consumed cumulatively since 2022.

**The subsidy is a capex rebate.** Incentive cash received in H1 2024 was $699M [C65], 6.0% [C66] of the $11,652M [C64] spent on capex. The award terms themselves were not retrievable from any filing this session — treat headline grant figures as unverified.

**Buffett's maxim presumes intact, estimable value.** Revenue is −31.38% [C77] versus 2021, gross margin 55.45% [C74] → 40.04% [C75] → 35.43% [C76] in Q2, Intel Foundry runs a −65.51% [C81] operating margin on a quarterly operating loss of $2,830M [C90], trailing EPS of $0.24 [C69] puts you at 83.79x [C71], and the whole equity is 4.16x [C79] the $20,605M [C78] 2019–21 average net income. That is an impairment multiple, not a trough multiple. The dividend is suspended from Q4.

I have no accounts on file, so I cannot see what share of your savings this would be.

---

**Conclusion.** The valuation premise holds: $INTC trades at 0.74x [C57] book, against 1.77x [C59] in March. The other two legs fail. The CHIPS money is a rebate against capex — $699M [C65] received versus $11,652M [C64] spent, 6.0% [C66] — and no filing in reach substantiates the award terms. Book is not a floor: it rose $9,256M [C61] on $11,861M [C62] of partner contributions while the quarter lost $1,610M [C86]. Earning power is the question, not sentiment: revenue −31.38% [C77] since 2021, gross margin 35.43% [C76], the foundry losing $2,830M [C90] a quarter, trailing free cash flow −$12,584M [C67], and no dividend from Q4. The fear follows filed numbers. What would change this: foundry losses narrowing from $2,830M [C90], free cash flow positive without partner contributions, an external leading-edge customer, gross margin durably above 40%. None of this shows the turnaround fails — only that it is unproven and unpriced on earnings.

This is research, not investment advice.

**They aren't the same bet, and the fee isn't the reason.**

$MSTR closed at $403.45 [E8:MSTR price:2024-11-25] against 386,700 bitcoin held [A13] worth $36.0bn [C40] at bitcoin's $93,102 [E8:BTC-USD price:2024-11-25]. Market value is $81.8bn [C39] — 2.27x the coin it owns [C41], a 127.3% premium [C59]. Pro forma debt is $7.18bn [C44], 19.9% of that coin value [C45]. The balance sheet is not the amplifier; the multiple is.

- **The outrun came from the multiple.** Over the window where both price series exist, $MSTR returned 241.8% [C5] against bitcoin's 53.1% [C6] — 4.55x the move [C72] — yet daily beta was 1.21x [C11] with 0.68 correlation [C12]. Volatility ran 99.2% [C9] versus 56.1% [C10]. On 2024-11-21 the stock fell 16.2% [C68] while bitcoin rose 4.4% [C69].
- **A price fall alone does not bankrupt it.** The bitcoin-collateralised 6.125% notes have been redeemed [E19], so there is no margin-call mechanism. Through 2022 it held 132,500 bitcoin [E25] against a 77.6% peak-to-trough decline [C78], with $43.8m of cash [E25], and survived. The coins stop covering the debt only at $18,572 per bitcoin [C48].
- **What breaks is the equity.** Repeat that drawdown: equity at 1.0x [A23] is $931m [C53], -98.9% from today [C54]. If bitcoin halves to $46,551 [C73] — a -50% coin return [A25] — the equity is -86.7% [C58]. Compressing to 1.0x [A23] needs bitcoin +127.3% just to stand still [C75]; with bitcoin flat that is a 56.0% loss [C83]. At 1.5x [A24] it needs +51.6% [C74].

**Bottom line.** A spot bitcoin ETF is bitcoin minus a fee. $MSTR is $36.0bn of bitcoin [C40] geared by a 2.27x multiple [C41] and a $7.18bn unsecured convertible stack [C44] [E19], funded by continuous issuance — $12.8bn of ATM capacity remains [C67]. A brutal crypto winter would not bankrupt the company; it would crush the equity through multiple compression and dilution, with the 2022 analogue at roughly -99% [C54]. The decisive variable is the premium, not the fee: a 0.25%/yr fee scenario [A18] costs 2.47% over ten years [C82], while a round trip to 1.0x [A23] costs 56.0% [C83]. Caveats: the fee is a scenario input [A18], debt is pro forma [A14], and the price statistics cover a bull window only.

*This is research, not investment advice.*

**The outperformance is leverage plus a premium, not a fee difference.** Over the window where both price series overlap, $MSTR returned +241.8% [C14] against bitcoin's +53.1% [C15] — a 4.55x [C16] multiple. It also ran 99.2% [C17] annualised volatility against bitcoin's 56.1% [C18], with a beta to bitcoin of 1.21x [C19], and fell 14.9% [C4] over the last three sessions while bitcoin fell 1.3% [C5].

You pay 2.84x [C51] net asset value: 64.8% [C69] of the price is premium, and premium going to zero with bitcoin flat is −64.8% [C70].

**On bankruptcy:** long-term debt was $4,211.9m [E6] at 30 September 2024, plus the convertible notes due 2029 carrying $3.0bn [A21] of principal at a 0% [C82] coupon. The coins are worth $36.0bn [C45], so debt is 20.0% [C52] of that asset. The only bitcoin-collateralised block is the 2028 secured notes at $500m [A24] of principal, against 14,890 coins pledged at end-2022 [E29]; that is 6.93% [C74] of the stack. Cash interest on it, $30.6m [A25], is 8.9% [C65] of trailing gross profit.

Equity NAV per share reaches zero at a bitcoin price of about $18,649.98 [C79], a fall of 79.97% [C80]. At the 2022 low of $15,460 [A26] the per-share figure in the report turns negative [C62]. The ATM sales disclosed in the 25 November 8-K — 5,597,849 shares for about $2.46bn of net proceeds in the week to 24 November — cover a date window, not a quantity [E23].

---

**Conclusion.** $MSTR beats a spot bitcoin ETF on the way up because it applies 1.21x [C19] beta to bitcoin and sells equity at 2.84x [C51] NAV to buy more coins: bitcoin per share rose 49.1% [C57] in eight weeks while diluted shares rose 38.7% [C66] year on year. That is a bet on the premium persisting, not on bitcoin alone. A crypto winter on its own is unlikely to bankrupt the company — the debt is long-dated, unsecured apart from the 6.93% [C74] collateralised against coins, and 2022's 77.59% [C81] bitcoin decline produced $1.286bn of impairment losses and a $1.470bn net loss rather than a filing [E17]. A winter takes the equity: NAV per share falls to $53.41 [C58] at a 50% bitcoin decline, and it closes the issuance window. Bankruptcy requires a maturity landing in a shut credit market, and the full maturity ladder was not retrievable from the filings available here; that remains the decisive gap.

This is research, not investment advice.

A sale at 31.5x earnings [C19] and a 3.28% free-cash-flow yield [C22] is at least as consistent with a valuation decision as with a verdict on AI, and the sale alone distinguishes neither.

**"iPhone 16 is a flop" isn't yet a claim about anything.** Apple's 10-Q and its 1 August earnings release describe Apple Intelligence as something that "will be available on certain iPhone, Mac and iPad devices" [E15] — future tense. A verdict on an unlaunched phone is a prediction. What *is* documented is real softness in the current lineup: iPhone revenue fell 0.94% [C4] and Greater China fell 6.54% [C5] in the June quarter. The concern has a seed; the conclusion is premature.

**"Lost the AI race" collides with the P&L.** June-quarter revenue rose 4.87% [C1] to a record for that quarter: products +1.62% [C2], Services +14.14% [C3]. Services are 28.2% of revenue [C23] at a 74.0% gross margin [C15] versus 35.3% for products [C14], which is why gross margin rose to 46.26% [C8] from 44.52% [C9]. Over eight years revenue compounded at 6.38% [C33] while gross margin went from 40.06% [C34] to 44.13% [C35].

**Against the Nokia test, that's the wrong direction.** Nokia died of deflating prices and margin, plus value migrating to a software layer it didn't own. Apple's margins are expanding and the software layer is its fastest-growing, highest-margin segment. The genuine bear case is price, not obsolescence: at 31.5x trailing earnings [C19] on trailing revenue growth of 0.44% to 29 June 2024 [C56], a delayed or underwhelming AI cycle costs you multiple, not existence. The tape shows no extinction pricing either: $AAPL closed at 207.23 [C58], up 25.59% from its 19 April close [C26] and 11.75% below its 16 July close of 234.82 [C60][C59].

Two limits worth stating plainly. Nokia isn't in the filer directory and web retrieval was unavailable, so the Nokia comparison above is a structural test of the mechanism of its decline, not a quantified side-by-side. And no Apple product figures exist yet for a phone that hasn't launched, so nothing here scores the upgrade cycle — the December quarter does. The quarterly R&D dollar figure in the report's June-quarter paragraph is listed in its verification notes and should be treated as unconfirmed; the R&D growth rate and its share of revenue are supported.

The iPhone 16 verdict is a forecast: Apple's own filings, through 2 August 2024, still describe Apple Intelligence as forthcoming [E15]. The "lost the AI race" thesis runs into a quarter where revenue grew 4.87% [C1], Services grew 14.14% [C3], and gross margin expanded to 46.26% [C8] — the opposite of Nokia's margin collapse, though I could not source Nokia's own figures to quantify the gap. **Short answer: two of the three claims describe things that had not happened yet on 2024-08-06, and the third is a portfolio decision being read as a business verdict.**

**"iPhone 16 is a flop"** — there is no iPhone 16 revenue in any filed result. The newest period in Apple's XBRL is the quarter ended 2024-06-29 [E3], which is the iPhone 15 cycle. In that quarter revenue rose 4.87% [C7] to a June-quarter record, gross margin reached 46.26% [C8] versus 44.52% [C9] a year earlier, and gross profit grew 8.97% [C74]. The claim is a forecast, not an observation.

**"Lost the AI race"** — unfalsifiable as posed; Apple discloses no AI revenue. What is observable: R&D up 7.58% [C41] to 9.33% of revenue [C56], and Apple Intelligence described in the 10-Q as a generative-model system integrated into iOS 18, macOS Sequoia and iPadOS 18, available on certain devices [E22]. The channel that matters is upgrade pull and Services pricing, and Services grew 14.14% [C32].

**"Buffett sold half"** — the first leg is in the filings: Berkshire's 13F shows Apple going from 905.56m [C60] to 789.37m shares [C59], a 12.83% cut [C81], filed 2024-05-15 — before any of the current AI criticism. The Q2 leg sits in a 10-Q filed 2024-08-03 that I could not retrieve in this session, so treat "half" as unverified rather than confirmed or denied.

**"Next Nokia"** — Nokia's failure ran through margin collapse; Apple's gross margin has gone from 37.82% in FY19 [C52] to 46.26% [C8] now, with TTM operating margin of 31.27% [C71] against 29.23% [C73] and $104.3bn of TTM free cash flow [C80]. The real bear case is different and better evidenced: revenue growth of 0.43% [C79] on a 31.5x trailing multiple [C26] and a 3.28% FCF yield [C55].

**Conclusion.** The evidence does not support an Apple-as-Nokia thesis. Revenue is flat rather than collapsing, gross margin is at a record, operating margin is expanding and TTM free cash flow is $104.3bn [C80], so the destruction mechanism that took Nokia down is absent from Apple's filed numbers. Two of the three viral claims are about events that did not exist on this date — no iPhone 16 revenue appears in any filing, and "losing the AI race" has no disclosed metric behind it — while the Berkshire trim of 12.83% [C81] began in Q1 2024, before the current criticism, and left Apple at 40.81% of Berkshire's reported 13F value [C82]. The report's figures, re-cited: the two sessions from the 29 October close took 40.7% off the stock [C78], to $29.11 [C77]. results.finalAssistantText:
**Short answer: it is not a dip in the ordinary sense — the price fell because the market lost the ability to value the company, not because it marked down a known cash-flow stream.**

**The move, corrected.** Close-to-close from 2024-10-29 to 2024-10-31 the stock fell -40.74% [C2], not more than 50% [U1]: -32.68% on the 30th [C3] and -11.97% on the 31st [C4], on 236m and 130m shares [E3]. Part of the apparent collapse on a chart is mechanical — the 10-for-1 forward split took effect at the start of October [E8], so the quoted price was divided by ten before the selloff began. Against the split-adjusted 2024-09-30 level the stock is down -30.09% [C6]. The real drawdown is from mid-year: -68.359% [C30] from the 2024-06-18 closing high of $92.00 [C29], which is that day's close restated for the split [E3][A12].

**What broke.** Ernst & Young resigned as auditor on 2024-10-24, mid-audit, saying it could "no longer be able to rely on management's and the Audit Committee's representations" and was "unwilling to be associated with the financial statements prepared by management" [E4]. EY had never issued a report on the company [E4]. The FY2024 10-K is unfiled and overdue [E5], Nasdaq issued a listing deficiency notice on 2024-09-17 [E11], and lenders pushed the audited-financials delivery date to 2024-11-27 while requiring a $250m term-loan prepayment and adding a $70m availability block [E8]. The board's forensic review is unfinished [E4].

**What you'd be paying.** The newest XBRL data is the March 2024 quarter. TTM revenue $11.82bn [C10], TTM diluted EPS $1.782 [C11], so 16.3x [C12] and 1.34x EV/revenue [C13]; on the vendor's June-quarter EPS the multiple is 14.1x [C15], but that feed conflicts with the company's own filings in most overlapping quarters, so treat the lower multiple as the weaker number. Growth is real — revenue +200.01% year over year in the March 2024 quarter [C25] — with thinning margins, gross margin 15.52% against 17.01% a year earlier, a -1.50pp change [C26][C27][C28], and heavy cash burn: -$2.22bn free cash flow across the December and March quarters [C17].

**Limits.** Two figures in the report's price narrative — the pre-split September close and its split-adjusted equivalent — were written as prose restatements rather than computed cells, so treat them as illustrative of the split mechanics only; the verified values are the percentages above. I could also find no source for press reporting on a federal probe, so nothing here rests on one. The deeper limit is structural: no auditor has signed the last seven months of numbers, so every valuation figure here is management's, unverified.

**Conclusion.** The -40.74% two-day fall [C2] is not a sentiment drawdown to fade; it is the market repricing an unauditable company. The decisive facts are EY's resignation language — it would not be associated with management's financial statements [E4] — the still-unfiled FY2024 10-K [E5], the Nasdaq deficiency notice [E11], and a lender deadline of 2024-11-27 with a $250m prepayment already demanded [E8]. Against that, the shares trade at 16.3x unaudited trailing EPS and 1.34x revenue [C12][C13], on a balance sheet with $2.12bn of cash against $85.6m of long-term debt as of March [E12] and -$2.22bn of free cash flow over two quarters [C17]. So the outcome is decided by the audit, not by the entry price: a clean opinion reprices this violently upward, a missed covenant date reprices it the other way. What remains uncertain is what the forensic review will find — precisely what cannot be known from the filings available today. This is research, not investment advice.

One figure in the report, "≈$39.3 billion" of iPhone revenue, is a rounding of the $39,296 million June-quarter line disclosed in the release's product table; it is not an independently sourced number.

Research, not investment advice.
